# Will a worn clutch ever completely fail to engage? If not, what will cause this?

When a clutch begins to slip due to organic material wear on the friction disk, it creates a progressive degradation in torque transfer. As the linings thin, the coefficient of friction drops, requiring more pedal travel or higher engine RPMs to achieve full engagement. However, a worn friction surface alone typically does not result in a complete failure where the transmission remains locked in neutral despite the clutch being fully depressed. The hydraulic actuation system is designed to apply maximum clamping force regardless of how thin the disk has become; it simply cannot overcome the reduced friction area to transmit power effectively, but it should still lock the flywheel and pressure plate together physically.

In your specific case involving a 1999 Mercedes SLK230, the symptom you described—where the clutch pedal travels fully to the floor yet the engine revs without moving the car even when stationary—is distinct from simple wear. This behavior suggests that the mechanical connection between the input shaft and the pressure plate has been severed or bypassed. Waiting too long to address slipping can indeed lead to catastrophic secondary damage, but usually not in a way that renders the primary engagement mechanism non-functional unless other components are involved.

The most probable culprit is failure of the release bearing (throw-out bearing) or the pilot bushing/bearing within the transmission. On many Mercedes models of this era, the release mechanism relies on a ball-and-socket type throw-out bearing that pushes against the diaphragm spring fingers of the pressure plate. If this bearing seizes in its housing due to prolonged exposure to heat and lack of lubrication from the slipping clutch, it can physically prevent the diaphragm springs from flexing inward. Without that flex, the friction disk never disengages from the flywheel when you press the pedal. You are essentially trying to spin a transmission input shaft while the clutch is mechanically locked in "clutch" mode by a stuck bearing.

Another possibility specific to your symptoms of worsening engagement over days is damage to the pilot bushing or the center of the pressure plate itself. If the pilot bearing has worn out completely, creating excessive radial play, it can cause the transmission input shaft to wobble violently during operation. In extreme cases, this misalignment can prevent the clutch fork from properly seating or allow the release mechanism to bind against the distorted surface. While less common than a seized bearing, a collapsed pilot bushing can effectively stop the engine from driving the transmission even when force is applied to the release lever.

The progression you observed—slipping worsening daily before total loss of engagement—is consistent with thermal runaway. As the clutch slips, it generates immense heat. This heat cooks the grease inside the release bearing and damages the pilot bushing seals. Once these components overheat, they expand and seize. By the time you replaced the friction assembly, the hydraulic system was likely functioning correctly (pushing the fork all the way), but the mechanical linkage at the end of that push failed to convert linear motion into rotational disengagement.

Before reinstalling a new clutch on an SLK230, it is critical to inspect the entire input shaft and release mechanism. If you install a fresh friction disk while a seized throw-out bearing remains in place, you risk snapping the new pressure plate fingers or damaging the flyface immediately upon first engagement attempt. Additionally, check the transmission pilot bushing for play; if the input shaft wobbles by more than 0.1mm, replacing the pilot bearing is mandatory to prevent premature failure of the new clutch kit.

If your vehicle still exhibits no movement despite full pedal travel after replacement, verify that the hydraulic slave cylinder and master cylinder are actually moving the fork the full distance required to compress the diaphragm springs. A collapsed slave cylinder would mimic a stuck release bearing externally but lacks the internal seizure characteristics. Addressing these mechanical failures is often more cost-effective than replacing the entire drivetrain assembly if caught early enough after the initial slip phase.
